title: Testing What Steers a Growing Axon
endLine: Place cues around growth cones; their motion separates attraction from repulsion.

scenes.tts: How do you test what steers a growing nerve fibre? That fibre is an axon, led by a flat, moving fan called the growth cone. Molecules outside, called guidance cues, pull or push it.
scenes.caption: How do you test what steers a growing nerve fibre? That fibre is an axon, led by a flat, moving fan called the growth cone. Molecules outside, called guidance cues, pull or push it.
scenes.visual: Top-down microscope view of a circular culture dish filling most of the frame height (schematic). A growing axon extends from the left edge, tipped by an animated growth cone whose thin spikes constantly wave and probe. Two soft glowing cue clouds drift above and below beside a bold question mark; concise high-contrast labels 'axon', 'growth cone', and 'guidance cues' appear right after each object settles and before it is named.
scenes.narration: How do you test what steers a growing nerve fibre? That fibre is an axon, led by a flat, moving fan called the growth cone. Molecules outside, called guidance cues, pull or push it.

scenes.visual: The culture dish stays in place and dims gently as the growth cone continues slow ambient probing (schematic). Centered title 'Testing What Steers a Growing Axon' fades in cleanly, holds, and fades out.

scenes.tts: The growth cone probes its surface with actin spikes, sheets, and cue-sensing receptors. When a cue hits one side more strongly, it turns toward or away. Cues act on contact or across distance, so each needs its own dish test.
scenes.caption: The growth cone probes its surface with actin spikes, sheets, and cue-sensing receptors. When a cue hits one side more strongly, it turns toward or away. Cues act on contact or across distance, so each needs its own dish test.
scenes.visual: Same culture dish zoomed slightly onto the growth cone (schematic). Parallel edge spikes ('actin spikes'), translucent webs between them ('sheets'), and rim markers ('receptors') highlight in sequence before being named. A bright cue cloud drifts to the upper rim and the cone steers upward; a second colour cloud on the lower rim pushes it away. Two small edge icons briefly show 'on contact' (fixed dots) and 'across distance' (drifting cloud), then clear.
scenes.narration: The growth cone probes its surface with actin spikes, sheets, and cue-sensing receptors. When a cue hits one side more strongly, it turns toward or away. Cues act on contact or across distance, so each needs its own dish test.

scenes.tts: To test cues across distance, embed living tissue pieces, called explants, in a collagen gel. A secreted cue spreads through the gel, drawing axons toward the source or pushing them away.
scenes.caption: To test cues across distance, embed living tissue pieces, called explants, in a collagen gel. A secreted cue spreads through the gel, drawing axons toward the source or pushing them away.
scenes.visual: The same dish fills with a faint three-dimensional fibrous mesh labelled 'collagen gel' (schematic). Two living tissue chunks ('explants') appear on opposite sides: the left explant sprouts probing axons while the right explant pulses out a drifting cloud of cue dots. As the cloud crosses the gel, axons curve toward the source ('attract'); the source tint switches to a repellent colour and axons curve away ('repel').
scenes.narration: To test cues across distance, embed living tissue pieces, called explants, in a collagen gel. A secreted cue spreads through the gel, drawing axons toward the source or pushing them away.

scenes.tts: To test surface cues, lay alternating narrow membrane lanes like a striped carpet. Place axons across the lanes so each growth cone meets border after border and chooses a lane.
scenes.caption: To test surface cues, lay alternating narrow membrane lanes like a striped carpet. Place axons across the lanes so each growth cone meets border after border and chooses a lane.
scenes.visual: The gel dissolves and the dish floor transforms into alternating vertical narrow lanes of two contrasting tints ('striped carpet', schematic). A strip of tissue sits along the left edge; growing axons advance rightward across border after border. At each tinted lane edge, probing growth cones visibly pause, retract spikes on the repellent border, and steer into the permissive lanes.
scenes.narration: To test surface cues, lay alternating narrow membrane lanes like a striped carpet. Place axons across the lanes so each growth cone meets border after border and chooses a lane.

scenes.tts: Flood a dish with repellent membranes, and responsive fans can collapse into thin tips within minutes. Release the cue from one pipette side, and the cone turns away. Every assay places cues around growth cones so motion separates attraction from repulsion.
scenes.caption: Flood a dish with repellent membranes, and responsive fans can collapse into thin tips within minutes. Release the cue from one pipette side, and the cone turns away. Every assay places cues around growth cones so motion separates attraction from repulsion.
scenes.visual: Same dish with a plain flat floor and a spread, probing growth cone (schematic). First, dark membrane speckles wash evenly over the whole bath; the spread fan folds inward into a thin blunt tip ('collapse'). Then the speckles clear, the fan spreads again, and a fine pipette enters from the right releasing a one-sided drifting cloud of dots; the growth cone bends cleanly left ('turning').
scenes.narration: Flood a dish with repellent membranes, and responsive fans can collapse into thin tips within minutes. Release the cue from one pipette side, and the cone turns away. Every assay places cues around growth cones so motion separates attraction from repulsion.

scenes.tts: Yet avoiding a lane can mislead. Migrating neural crest cells carry eff receptors, and avoid stripes of their partner, ephrin B one. A sceptic says that stripe is simply a poor surface. Now add soluble ephrin B one, leaving the stripe surface unchanged. If avoidance is active repulsion, what happens?
scenes.caption: Yet avoiding a lane can mislead. Migrating neural crest cells carry Eph receptors, and avoid stripes of their partner, ephrin-B1. A sceptic says that stripe is simply a poor surface. Now add soluble ephrin-B1, leaving the stripe surface unchanged. If avoidance is active repulsion, what happens?
scenes.visual: The dish floor returns to alternating lanes labelled 'ephrin-B1' and neutral (schematic). Migrating chick neural crest cells, with small rim markers labelled 'Eph receptors', travel along the neutral lanes. A sceptic tag briefly reads 'poor surface?' over the tinted stripe. Then glowing dots labelled 'soluble ephrin-B1' drift evenly into the bath while the stripe floor stays visibly unchanged. At the top, the question card appears: 'If avoidance is active repulsion, what happens?'
scenes.narration: Yet avoiding a lane can mislead. Migrating neural crest cells carry Eph receptors, and avoid stripes of their partner, ephrin-B1. A sceptic says that stripe is simply a poor surface. Now add soluble ephrin-B1, leaving the stripe surface unchanged. If avoidance is active repulsion, what happens?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause in the same striped dish (schematic). The question 'If avoidance is active repulsion, what happens?' remains on screen while soluble ephrin-B1 dots drift gently across the bath, cells hover near a stripe border, and a quiet progress bar slowly fills along the bottom.

scenes.tts: The cells cross the stripes and spread evenly, as the 1997 chick study showed. Free ephrin fills eff receptors everywhere, so the border no longer reads as different. A merely poor surface would still be avoided, because the stripe itself is unchanged. A protein that does not bind eff receptors should leave avoidance intact.
scenes.caption: The cells cross the stripes and spread evenly, as the 1997 chick study showed. Free ephrin fills Eph receptors everywhere, so the border no longer reads as different. A merely poor surface would still be avoided, because the stripe itself is unchanged. A protein that does not bind Eph receptors should leave avoidance intact.
scenes.visual: Same striped dish (schematic). Soluble ephrin-B1 dots fill receptor markers uniformly around each cell rim; the border signal disappears and cells glide smoothly across both lanes ('1997 chick study'). A brief corner comparison, labelled 'expected', contrasts a 'poor surface' (cells still avoid) and a 'non-binding control' (different-shaped dots drift past empty receptors while avoidance persists).
scenes.narration: The cells cross the stripes and spread evenly, as the 1997 chick study showed. Free ephrin fills Eph receptors everywhere, so the border no longer reads as different. A merely poor surface would still be avoided, because the stripe itself is unchanged. A protein that does not bind Eph receptors should leave avoidance intact.

scenes.tts: Layout, dose, and exposure time also shape whether a cone turns or collapses. Receptors decide whether a cone answers at all. Internal state, such as cyclic G M P level, can decide which way. And a gel shows steering across distance, not the molecule itself.
scenes.caption: Layout, dose, and exposure time also shape whether a cone turns or collapses. Receptors decide whether a cone answers at all. Internal state, such as cyclic GMP level, can decide which way. And a gel shows steering across distance, not the molecule itself.
scenes.visual: Same dish (schematic). A single growth cone first turns gently away from a low one-sided pipette cloud, then collapses under a dense uniform bath ('layout, dose, time'). Rim markers labelled 'receptors' light up before the cone reacts. Inside the cone, a simple bar gauge labelled 'cyclic GMP' (schematic, no direction implied) changes level and the same cue switches between turning away and turning toward. The view pulls back to the collagen gel dish with a question mark over the cloud labelled 'which molecule?'.
scenes.narration: Layout, dose, and exposure time also shape whether a cone turns or collapses. Receptors decide whether a cone answers at all. Internal state, such as cyclic GMP level, can decide which way. And a gel shows steering across distance, not the molecule itself.

scenes.tts: In 1988, Marc Tessier-Lavigne and colleagues, in Thomas Jessell's laboratory, set embryonic rat spinal cord explants in collagen gel. Something from the floor plate crossed the gel, drawing midline-crossing axons; it was later named netrin. In 1990, Jonathan Raper and Josef Kapfhammer added embryonic brain membranes to chick dorsal root ganglion neurons. Cones collapsed within minutes, recovering once the membranes were gone.

scenes.visual: The dish splits cleanly into two carried-world panels (schematic). Left panel ('1988 · Tessier-Lavigne, Jessell lab'): collagen gel with 'dorsal spinal cord' and 'floor plate' explants as a drifting unnamed cue cloud ('?', later relabelled 'netrin') draws commissural axons across. Right panel ('1990 · Raper & Kapfhammer'): chick 'dorsal root ganglion' growth cones fold into thin tips when 'brain membranes' wash in, then re-open into probing fans once the membranes wash away.
scenes.narration: In 1988, Marc Tessier-Lavigne and colleagues, in Thomas Jessell's laboratory, set embryonic rat spinal cord explants in collagen gel. In 1990, Jonathan Raper and Josef Kapfhammer added embryonic brain membranes to chick dorsal root ganglion neurons. Cones collapsed within minutes, recovering once the membranes were gone.

scenes.tts: In 1987, Jochen Walter, Friedrich Bonhoeffer and colleagues striped anterior and posterior chick tectum membranes for retinal axons. In 1995, Drescher, Bonhoeffer and colleagues used that assay to purify a posterior tectum repellent. It is now called ephrin A five. Across gels, stripes, and baths, growth cones show what attracts or repels.
scenes.caption: In 1987, Jochen Walter, Friedrich Bonhoeffer and colleagues striped anterior and posterior chick tectum membranes for retinal axons. In 1995, Drescher, Bonhoeffer and colleagues used that assay to purify a posterior tectum repellent. It is now called ephrin-A5. Across gels, stripes, and baths, growth cones show what attracts or repels.
scenes.visual: The dish merges back into the full-frame alternating striped carpet (schematic) with lanes labelled 'anterior' and 'posterior tectum' ('1987 · Walter & Bonhoeffer'); a strip of retina sends axons that meet border after border (no lane preference drawn for 1987). A highlight tag pulls a protein from the posterior lane, labelled 'ephrin-A5' ('1995 · Drescher & Bonhoeffer'), and a retinal growth cone collapses and retreats at its edge. In the closing beat, one living growth cone steers smoothly as faint rings of gel, stripes, and bath cycle gently around it.

scenes.visual: The culture dish fades out into a clean dark end card displaying only the take-home rule in large high-contrast text: 'Place cues around growth cones; their motion separates attraction from repulsion.'
